verdict_reasoning: Demand is shown and the problem is stated, so levels 1a and 1b pass. Level 2 has open design points the list must settle before code review. Message #1 says an idle session can hold back datfrozenxid with no remedy (replication-ondisk-1). No one has written the comparison with the competing series that message #25 asked for (maintenance-fit-3). Nothing fails loudly when code bypasses the session overlay (prior-attempts-1). All are fixable.

brief.title: Global temporary tables with shared definition and session-local data
brief.problem: Postgres has no table whose definition is permanent and shared while its data is private to each session. Reviewers named two groups who want this: users moving from other systems, and workloads that use temporary tables heavily and fragment the catalogs.
brief.proposed_design: `create global temp table` adds a relpersistence 'g' table that gets local storage and local buffers the first time a session uses it. A shared hash table tracks use across backends and blocks a rewrite or scan of a table that another session is using. Per-session filenode, statistics, frozen XIDs and index valid/ready flags live in backend memory, column and extended statistics go into new global temporary catalogs, and each PGPROC publishes tempfrozenxid so that datfrozenxid can advance.
user_visible_surface: Syntax `CREATE GLOBAL TEMP[ORARY] TABLE` and `CREATE GLOBAL TEMP SEQUENCE`; `GLOBAL` no longer ignored
New pg_class columns: reloncommit, and relpersistence value 'g'; psql \d shows the ON COMMIT action
New catalogs pg_temp_statistic and pg_temp_statistic_ext_data; pg_stats, pg_stats_ext, pg_stats_ext_exprs include them
pg_stat_activity columns tempfrozenxid and tempminmxid; new `DISCARD GLOBAL TEMP`; ambuildempty() gains a fork number argument
author_claims: The design avoids the problems of an earlier, older global temporary table patch.
Each session runs VACUUM now and then, so datfrozenxid can still advance.
Keeping session state in memory removed fragile flushing code and cut the series from 11 to 9 patches.
Indexes that are not ready in a session close the partial uniqueness problem without blocking CREATE INDEX in other sessions.
Saving ON COMMIT to pg_class is useful and could go in on its own.
brief.thread_state: Many reviewers tested the series and found bugs, which the author fixed through v12; Haibo Yan then posted fixes for two ON CONFLICT bugs and raised an open policy question on ADD CONSTRAINT ... USING INDEX. Andrew Dunstan has a competing patch series, and no one has written the comparison of the two designs that John Naylor asked for.
unclear: The proposal does not say what stops an idle session that once used a global temporary table from blocking wraparound protection, since autovacuum cannot process it.
No reviewer has compared this design with Andrew Dunstan's series, which stores ON COMMIT as a reloption and handles wraparound differently.
The material gives no measurements of catalog bloat, of the cost of the shared hash table, or of planning overhead.
The proposal does not settle whether global temporary tables should support inheritance, which earlier messages raised and left open.
The proposal does not say how pg_upgrade and physical standbys handle global temporary relations; one reviewer found errors on a standby.

objections.title: Idle sessions that used a global temporary table can block wraparound protection
objections.failure_scenario: A connection pooler keeps 200 backends open for weeks, and each touched a global temporary table once. Their tempfrozenxid values stop datfrozenxid and clog truncation from advancing. Autovacuum cannot fix this, so the DBA learns about it from wraparound warnings and must find and terminate or DISCARD each backend.
objections.argument: Message #1 and the 0006 commit message state that datfrozenxid advances only if each session runs VACUUM from time to time, and autovacuum is excluded. Local temporary tables have the same weakness, but with a global temporary table any application session that reads a shared definition can pin the horizon. Message #37 item 10 also reports that a database-wide VACUUM opens every global temporary table. Exposing tempfrozenxid in pg_stat_activity (message #28) helps diagnosis but does not provide protection.
objections.author_must_show: What bounds the age of tempfrozenxid for a backend that is idle but still connected, and is a backend that never wrote to a global temporary table exempt from it?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 states the problem and says it is not clear what can be done; v12 adds only monitoring columns and a manual DISCARD. Local temporary tables share the weakness, which lowers the weight, but message #37 item 10 widens the exposure and has no visible answer.

objections.title: Permanent catalog shape chosen before the two designs are compared
objections.failure_scenario: The project releases reloncommit, relpersistence 'g' and two new global temporary catalogs. If Andrew Dunstan's approach, with ON COMMIT stored as a reloption and different wraparound handling, later proves better, the switch requires catalog changes plus pg_upgrade and pg_dump compatibility code for the released format.
objections.argument: Message #4 says neither design is a clear winner on the catalog or on wraparound. In message #25 John Naylor asked for a comparison of the operational and maintenance tradeoffs, and no one has written it. The catalog choice has already changed twice in this thread: pg_temp_class and pg_temp_index were added and then removed (messages #40 and #43). Catalog columns and relpersistence values are hard to take back once released.
objections.author_must_show: Where do the two series differ on catalog layout and wraparound handling, and why is this design's choice better for long-term maintenance?

critic.reasoning: John Naylor asked for the comparison in message #25 and the thread contains none. The cost of a later switch is smaller than stated, because catalog columns can change between major versions and pg_dump emits ON COMMIT as syntax.

objections.title: Session-local pg_class and pg_index overlay may repeat the earlier maintainability objection
objections.failure_scenario: A future patch, or an extension, reads pg_index.indisready or pg_class.relfilenode directly instead of through the GetEffective_* helpers. On a global temporary table that code then acts on another session's base value, for example by skipping an index or trusting stale freeze data. No test or assertion fails until a user hits it.
objections.argument: The earliest global temporary table attempt [P1] was turned away as unmaintainable, with a call for a generic way to split catalog state into local and non-local parts. v11 dropped pg_temp_class and pg_temp_index in favor of an in-memory overlay applied in ScanPgRelation and a set of effective-value helpers (message #41, message #43). Reviewers have already found consumers that bypassed the overlay: a direct indisvalid read in repack.c (message #44) and an infer_arbiter_indexes assertion that is now wrong for global temporary tables (message #46). The thread does not say how such misses would be caught after commit.
objections.author_must_show: What mechanism, such as an assertion or a check, makes a direct read of a session-local pg_class or pg_index field fail loudly for a global temporary relation?

critic.reasoning: Messages #44 and #46 show two readers that bypassed the overlay, both found by review, and the material names no check that fails loudly. [P1] supports this only loosely, because its recorded reason concerns a different design.

objections.title: DISCARD ALL does not clear global temporary table data
objections.failure_scenario: A connection pooler resets each server connection with DISCARD ALL before giving it to the next client. Client A fills a global temporary table and disconnects. Client B gets the same backend and reads A's rows, and nothing reports an error.
objections.argument: Message #37 showed that rows and sequence values survive DISCARD ALL. Message #39 answers with a separate DISCARD GLOBAL TEMP that works independently of DISCARD TEMP, and the brief lists it as new syntax. The material does not say whether DISCARD ALL now includes it. Poolers rely on DISCARD ALL meaning that no session state carries over to the next client.
objections.author_must_show: Does DISCARD ALL discard global temporary data and sequence state, and if not, how does a pooler user learn that DISCARD ALL is no longer a full reset?

critic.reasoning: Message #37 shows rows and sequence state surviving DISCARD ALL, and message #39 describes DISCARD GLOBAL TEMP as independent of DISCARD TEMP. The visible prose does not say whether DISCARD ALL now includes it, so the pooler scenario stands.

objections.title: pg_class.relfrozenxid of zero breaks existing wraparound monitoring queries
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA runs the wraparound query from the maintenance chapter, or a monitoring tool built on it. Each global temporary table has relkind 'r' and relfrozenxid 0, so age() returns its maximum value. The alert fires at once, and the real per-session horizon sits in a set-returning function the tool never calls.
objections.argument: Patch 0006 sets pg_class.relfrozenxid and relminmxid to zero for global temporary relations. The query in maintenance.sgml still filters on relkind IN ('r','m') without change. relpages and reltuples likewise become values that pg_gtr_info() overrides, so tools that read pg_class get base values with no sign that these are not the real ones. Haibo Yan raised the base-versus-effective model in message #15, and the answer so far is documentation, which existing tools will not read.
objections.author_must_show: How do the documented wraparound query and common external tools that read pg_class.relfrozenxid avoid reporting every global temporary table at maximum age?

critic.reasoning: age() returns its maximum for an invalid XID, and the maintenance.sgml hunk keeps the `relkind IN ('r', 'm')` query unchanged. The documented query would report every global temporary table at maximum age.

other_surviving.title: Default ON COMMIT action differs from the standard and Oracle
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A user ports Oracle DDL that has no ON COMMIT clause, as migration users would. Oracle and the SQL standard delete rows at commit, but here the rows stay. Later transactions in the same session see stale rows, and the user finds out from wrong results.
other_surviving.argument: Message #21 shows that a global temporary table without ON COMMIT gets reloncommit 'p'. Migration from other systems is the main stated demand (messages #5 and #8), and the standard spelling now claims this semantics. Local temporary tables already deviate from the standard here, but GLOBAL is a new contract. Once released, changing its default would silently change the behaviour of existing DDL.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Why should CREATE GLOBAL TEMPORARY TABLE default to PRESERVE ROWS when the standard and Oracle default to DELETE ROWS, and where is this deviation documented?

critic.reasoning: The default copies local temporary tables, whose deviation from the standard is already documented, and that lowers the weight. The thread still does not weigh it for the migration users it names as the main demand, and the porting scenario is concrete.

other_surviving.title: Physical standby behaviour for global temporary tables is not defined
other_surviving.failure_scenario: An operator runs a monitoring query such as pg_total_relation_size() over pg_class on a hot standby. Once the database has a global temporary table, the query fails, as message #37 item 5 shows. Read-only sessions on the standby also have no defined rule for first-use storage, local statistics or the shared usage table.
other_surviving.argument: Message #37 item 5 reports a failing COMMIT and a failing catalog-wide size query on a standby. The thread does not answer that report directly, and message #40 only claims that all outstanding issues were fixed. The commit messages list what is forbidden on the primary but do not say what a standby session may do with a global temporary table. Examples are reads of an empty table, first-use initialisation, and ANALYZE, which is impossible on a standby.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What exactly may a hot standby session do with a global temporary table, and which tests show that catalog-wide queries on a standby work?

critic.reasoning: Message #40 says all outstanding issues were fixed, and patches 0002 and 0004 touch 001_stream_rep.pl, so some standby testing exists. The visible prose still does not state what a standby session may do with a global temporary table.

other_surviving.title: A role without privileges can register usage and block the owner's DDL
other_surviving.failure_scenario: An unprivileged role runs a database-wide VACUUM, which opens every global temporary table before any ownership check, and then leaves the session idle. The table owner's rewriting ALTER TABLE or ADD CONSTRAINT then fails with "in use by another session". No lock appears in pg_locks, and the owner cannot end the session without pg_signal_backend.
other_surviving.argument: Message #37 (point 10) reports that VACUUM, ANALYZE, REINDEX DATABASE, REPACK ALL and reads of pg_sequences open all global temporary tables or sequences, which adds entries to the shared usage hash. Messages #39 to #45 do not answer that point. The usage entry has no timeout. It also pins tempfrozenxid. So a role with no grant on the table can, for as long as its session lasts, block DDL by the owner and hold back datfrozenxid.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Are usage entries recorded only after the privilege check passes, and how can an owner who is not superuser find and clear a session that blocks their DDL?

critic.reasoning: The material does not show VACUUM opening relations before its permission check, so that part of the scenario is unsupported. Message #37 item 10 is still unanswered, and the functions shown report only the current session's usage, so an owner cannot find the blocking session.

other_surviving.title: No measurements of overhead for sessions that never use the feature
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A busy OLTP system that creates no global temporary tables upgrades to the release with this feature. It now runs the invalidation check at every transaction and command start, and every database-wide VACUUM scans all PGPROC entries. No one notices a regression until users compare benchmarks after release.
other_surviving.argument: Message #43 moves ProcessInvalidatedGlobalTempRelations to transaction start and command start. Message #22 adds a PGPROC scan under ProcArrayLock to vac_update_datfrozenxid. v12 also adds two fields to PGPROC and turns pg_stats and pg_stats_ext into UNION ALL views. The brief notes that the material contains no measurements, so the cost for non-users is unknown.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What do pgbench and catalog-heavy benchmarks show for a cluster with no global temporary tables, before and after the series?

critic.reasoning: Message #43 puts invalidation processing at every transaction and command start, a path all sessions run, and the material has no measurements. The VACUUM-time PGPROC scan is not a hot path, so the request reduces to numbers for the command-start check.

refuted.title: Existing CREATE GLOBAL TEMP scripts change meaning on upgrade
refuted.failure_scenario: An application runs create global temp table tmp_x (...) on commit drop at the start of each session. Today this gives a local temporary table plus a warning. After upgrade, ON COMMIT DROP is rejected, and without it the first session creates a permanent definition, so later sessions fail with "relation already exists".
refuted.argument: The documentation hunk removes the note that GLOBAL "presently makes no difference". Patch 0002 rejects ON COMMIT DROP for global temporary tables. Statements that run today get new semantics after upgrade without asking for them. The thread does not discuss existing users of the GLOBAL keyword, a migration path, or a release-note warning.
refuted.author_must_show: What happens on upgrade to applications that already write CREATE GLOBAL TEMP TABLE, and how are they warned before their behaviour changes?

critic.reasoning: Postgres has emitted a deprecation warning for GLOBAL in temporary table creation for many releases. The CREATE TABLE compatibility section says a later version might adopt the standard meaning, so existing users have had the warning the objection asks for.

refuted.title: pg_class.relfrozenxid of zero for tables breaks freeze monitoring
refuted.failure_scenario: A wraparound check runs the documented query age(relfrozenxid) over relkind 'r' rows. Each global temporary table reports an age of 2147483647, so alerts fire. Freeze scripts that then run VACUUM FREEZE on these tables create session storage in their own session for no benefit.
refuted.argument: 0006 sets pg_class.relfrozenxid and relminmxid to zero for every global temporary relation (message #22). Until now a zero value meant that the relation is not a table. age() of an invalid XID returns INT_MAX. The maintenance.sgml hunk keeps the query that filters relkind IN ('r','m') and does not warn that global temporary tables need to be excluded. pg_class.relfilenode and relpages also stop describing the real storage, which changes the meaning of a catalog that many external tools read.
refuted.author_must_show: How should existing monitoring and freeze tools that read pg_class.relfrozenxid recognise and handle global temporary tables, and will the documented queries be changed to match?

refuted.title: Using a global temporary table may bypass the TEMP privilege
refuted.failure_scenario: A DBA revokes TEMP on a database from PUBLIC to stop users creating session-local storage. A role with only SELECT and INSERT on a global temporary table fills it, uses temp_buffers and local files, and pins datfrozenxid while idle. The DBA learns about it when the wraparound warnings start.
refuted.argument: Today the TEMP privilege controls who can create session-local relations. Global temporary tables create per-session storage on first use, which message #1 and the 0002 commit message describe, but none of the material says whether that first use checks TEMP. If it does not, revoking TEMP no longer limits session-local storage or the frozen-XID holdback that message #1 describes for temporary tables. If it does, users with privileges on the table will see errors, and the docs need to say so.
refuted.author_must_show: Does the first use of a global temporary table in a session require the TEMP privilege on the database, and if not, why is that the right default?

critic.reasoning: TEMP governs creating objects in a session's temporary schema; it is not a limit on storage use. A role granted INSERT on any table can already fill storage, and creating the global temporary table needs CREATE on a regular schema, so no privilege is bypassed.

refuted.title: Session overlay of pg_class and pg_index fields fails silently when bypassed
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch reads pg_index.indisready or pg_class.relfrozenxid straight from the syscache. For a global temporary table that read returns the shared value, not the session value. The bug shows up only when two sessions use the same table, as the TRUNCATE horizon bug in message #19 and the repack.c read in message #44 did.
refuted.argument: v12 keeps about ten pg_class and pg_index fields in backend memory and overlays them in ScanPgRelation and a few GetEffective_* helpers, so every other reader has to know to use those helpers. Missed sites were found by review, not by tests: message #19, message #44, and the planner assertion in message #46. Haibo's audit in message #41 checks the code at one point in time and does nothing for future readers. [P1] records the earlier design as unmaintainable for the same overlay pattern.
refuted.author_must_show: Other than reviewer audits, what catches a new reader of these pg_class or pg_index fields that bypasses the session overlay?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1. Its claim that [P1] rejected "the same overlay pattern" is also not in the recorded reason for [P1].

refuted.title: Idle sessions can hold back datfrozenxid with no automatic remedy
refuted.failure_scenario: A pooled connection touches one global temporary table, or runs a database-wide VACUUM, and then sits idle for weeks. Its tempfrozenxid keeps datfrozenxid from advancing, and autovacuum cannot help. The DBA finds out from wraparound warnings and has to locate and terminate the backend by hand.
refuted.argument: Message #1 states this problem and says it is not clear what can be done. v12 adds only manual tools: the pg_stat_activity columns and DISCARD GLOBAL TEMP. Message #37 reported that a database-wide VACUUM opens every global temporary table, and the material does not show whether v12 changed that. Messages #41 and #43 leave the frozen-XID policy unchanged. Local temporary tables have the same weakness, but here any session that touches a shared object can trigger it.
refuted.author_must_show: Without action by an administrator, what stops an idle session that once opened a global temporary table from holding back datfrozenxid indefinitely?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows the relcache, catalog and VACUUM freeze-horizon code. The material does not mark any participant as a committer.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the session overlay of pg_class and pg_index fields, the shared usage hash, the PGPROC freeze fields, two new catalogs and the ambuildempty() change. Released syntax and catalog shape stay indefinitely.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted twelve versions in under five months and fixed the bugs reviewers reported, which suggests he stays for fixes.

priority.reason: Demand is shown by two independent series, earlier attempts [P1][P3][P4] and users citing migration and catalog bloat. The nine patches touch the relcache, VACUUM, the planner and every index access method, and the wraparound and design-comparison questions are open.

provisional_note: Without the code, this review could not check whether DISCARD ALL covers global temporary data, when usage entries are registered relative to privilege checks, how pg_upgrade handles these relations, or what the command-start invalidation check costs.

precedents_retrieved.title: Global temporary table
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add global temporary tables to PostgreSQL: a table definition stored once in the catalog, with each session getting its own private data files, local buffers, statistics and relfrozenxid tracking, kept in session-local hash tables plus a shared-memory hash that tracks which backends use each table. DDL on such a table would be allowed only when no other session holds data in it, and operations that change the relfilenode (VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER) would be disabled.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund held that the patch could not be merged with anything close to its current design, calling it unmaintainable, and said fundamental design work was needed first, possibly through a generic way to split catalog tables into local and non-local storage. Robert Haas found the patch too big and unpolished to review: one large code drop with weak comments and code quality, where reviewers kept finding crash bugs. He asked that it be split into independently committable patches and said reaching a committable state may require a near-total rewrite. Given these two opinions that it could not be reviewed effectively as it stood, the entry was marked Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Forbid accessing other session's temporary tables
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a check in relation_open that rejects any access to another session's temporary tables. The author found that inserts into another session's temp table could succeed, and each session then saw only its own rows.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew it after Andrey M. Borodin pointed to an earlier thread with a report and a proposed fix for the same problem. Before that, Tom Lane objected that the check in relation_open would block access to another session's temp table metadata, which operations such as drop need. He said only access to the table contents should be blocked.

Accessing the metadata of other temp tables is fine, and indeed
necessary for operations like dropping them.  It's access to
the table contents that needs to be blocked.

precedents_retrieved.title: Global temporary tables
precedents_retrieved.summary: Introduce "global temporary" tables (CREATE GLOBAL TEMP TABLE / CREATE SESSION TABLE), similar to Oracle's, whose definition is shared in the catalog by all backends while each backend's data is private and discarded at session end. The initial design accessed this data through shared buffers to avoid catalog bloat and to allow parallel queries and connection-pooler session migration; a later, simpler version used private buffers and left parallel queries and replica use out of scope.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch was waiting on author for the whole commitfest, probably because it no longer applied, and there was little activity, so the commitfest manager marked it returned with feedback. He said the feature was not considered undesirable and suggested combining efforts with a separate global temporary tables thread where most of the discussion was happening. Earlier design objections, such as Craig Ringer's to using shared buffers for temporary data, are visible but are not given as the reason for closing.

precedents_retrieved.summary: Add global temporary tables to PostgreSQL: a single shared pg_class definition (relpersistence 'g') whose data lives in per-session files and local buffers that are created on first use and removed at session end. Statistics, relfrozenxid and storage tracking are kept in session-local hash tables, with a shared-memory hash used to coordinate DDL against sessions that use the table.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The entry was marked Withdrawn on the same day the author posted a rebased version fixing the whitespace problems and the relcache reference leak that Pavel Stehule had reported, and the thread shows review still ongoing rather than an objection to the design.

precedents_retrieved.title: Temporary tables that do not bloat pg_catalog (a.k.a fast temp tables)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch added a new kind of temporary table (CREATE FAST TEMP TABLE) whose catalog information is kept in the creating backend's memory instead of in pg_catalog. The goal was to avoid pg_catalog bloat and the autovacuum work caused by applications that create and drop many temporary tables.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas objected that if the catalog entries live only in backend-private memory, other sessions cannot see the dependencies, so objects the temporary table depends on (for example functions used in indexes, triggers or defaults) can be dropped by other backends. Without globally visible dependency entries the design was not seen as workable. He also objected that the patch adds an in-memory heap implementation inside low-level heapam code paths instead of using a proper storage API, which he considered not maintainable. Alternative designs discussed later in the thread were judged to address the bloat problem only partly.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow tablespaces on RAM-based partitions for temporary objects
precedents_retrieved.summary: Bruce Momjian asked whether temp_tablespaces may point at storage that does not survive a restart, such as /tmp or a ramdisk, and whether to document this. The thread then moved to a TODO item for a new kind of tablespace that holds only temporary (and possibly unlogged) tables and is rebuilt empty at startup.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Claudio Freire noted that a tablespace whose directory structure is lost at restart stops the server from booting, and Andres Freund said that allowing unlogged tables adds work to recreate files and init forks. The visible thread ends with the ideas recorded as TODO items and a discussion of keyword names, not with a rejection.

precedents_retrieved.title: We broke the defense against accessing other sessions' temp tables
precedents_retrieved.summary: Since Postgres 17, a superuser can read another session's temp table and get wrong results instead of the error "cannot access temporary tables of other sessions", because the read stream path skips the check in ReadBufferExtended(). Tom Lane proposed moving the check into PinBufferForBlock(), and Thomas Munro suggested checking once in read_stream_begin_relation() with an assertion in PinBufferForBlock().
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last messages point to an overlapping patch already in the commitfest (patch 5379), which Thomas Munro said he would look at.

precedents_retrieved.title: Prepare Transaction support for ON COMMIT DROP temporary tables
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch allows PREPARE TRANSACTION when every temporary table the transaction accessed was created with ON COMMIT DROP. PreCommit_on_commit_actions() drops those tables before the prepare, so the existing check against temporary tables in prepared transactions is relaxed for this case.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier showed that after creating an ON COMMIT DROP temp table and preparing, a client can disconnect but the backend stays waiting for a lock on its temporary schema until COMMIT PREPARED. The patch also does not handle the case where the temp table creates the session's temporary schema, and Tom Lane noted that tables without an ON COMMIT clause are not tracked. The entry was returned with feedback because more work was needed.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums"
Reverted commit(s): Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 2aa6e33, that added a fast path to skip
anti-wraparound and non-aggressive autovacuum jobs (these have no sense
as anti-wraparound implies aggressive).  With a cluster using a high
amount of relations with a portion of them being heavily updated, this
could cause autovacuum to lock down, with autovacuum workers attempting
repeatedly those jobs on the same relations for the same database, that
just kept being skipped.  This lock down can be solved with a manual
VACUUM FREEZE.

Justin King has reported one environment where the issue happened, and
Julien Rouhaud and I have been able to reproduce it in a second
environment.  With a very aggressive autovacuum_freeze_max_age,
triggering those jobs with pgbench is a matter of minutes, and hitting
the lock down is a lot harder (my local tests failed to do that).

Note that anti-wraparound and non-aggressive jobs can only be triggered
on a subset of shared catalogs:
- pg_auth_members
- pg_authid
- pg_database
- pg_replication_origin
- pg_shseclabel
- pg_subscription
- pg_tablespace
While the lock down was possible down to v12, the root cause of those
jobs is a much older issue, which needs more analysis.

Bonus thanks to Andres Freund for the discussion.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert refactoring of restore command code to shell_restore.c
precedents_retrieved.summary: Revert refactoring of restore command code to shell_restore.c
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commits 24c35ec and 57169ad.  PreRestoreCommand() and
PostRestoreCommand() need to be put closer to the system() call calling
a restore_command, as they enable in_restore_command for the startup
process which would in turn trigger an immediate proc_exit() in the
SIGTERM handler.  Perhaps we could get rid of this behavior entirely,
but 24c35ec has made the window where the flag is enabled much larger
than it was, and any Postgres-like actions (palloc, etc.) taken by code
paths while the flag is enabled could lead to more severe issues in the
shutdown processing.

Note that curculio has showed that there are much more problems in this
area, unrelated to this change, actually, hence the issues related to
that had better be addressed first.  Keeping the code of HEAD in line
with the stable branches should make that a bit easier.

Per discussion with Andres Freund and Nathan Bossart.

roaster_notes.note: Only the [P1] maintainability reason still applies. [P5]'s reason about invisible dependencies does not apply, because the definitions here stay in the shared catalogs. [P9] has no recorded reason.
Objections are limited to the user-facing contract. pg_dump round-trip of ON COMMIT was fixed in message #36, and the material does not let me check pg_upgrade handling.
WAL is not involved because global temporary tables are always unlogged. Logical replication is excluded through publication and subscription checks, which the thread settled.

Statistics exposure looks handled: pg_temp_statistic is limited to superuser, and pg_stats filters rows by privilege. Publications and subscriptions are rejected for global temporary tables. These points could not be checked without the code.

Nothing in core gives a shared definition with session-local data. Local temp tables, created per session, give private data but keep the catalog churn that message #8 names as the main problem. Extensions that emulate this by creating a local temp table on first use have the same churn. They also cannot change relpersistence, local buffers, per-session statistics or the datfrozenxid calculation without core changes, so core placement is justified.

The material shows real, lasting demand: two independent implementations (messages #1, #2), several earlier attempts since 2019 [P1][P3][P4], the SQL-standard syntax, and users citing migration (#5), catalog bloat (#8) and production workflows (#11, #24). Costs that reach non-users, such as the ambuildempty() signature change and pg_stats becoming a UNION ALL view, are design questions for other angles.
